context_blurb:
Scientists give three words exact meanings: hypothesis, theory and law. In everyday talk people mix them up, as when someone waves an idea away as just a theory. In science each word does a different job: a hypothesis is an idea to test, a law sums up a pattern, and a theory explains why nature behaves as it does.

A hypothesis is a testable idea about what will happen, and it is often, though not always, put in the form "If..., then...". A boy who guesses that longer wings carry a paper plane farther can test his hypothesis by folding planes with short and long wings and measuring their glides.

Some observation must be able to show whether a hypothesis is right or wrong. The astronomer Carl Sagan once imagined telling a friend that his garage held a fire-breathing dragon. Each time the friend proposed a test, Sagan had an excuse: the dragon is invisible; it floats, so flour on the floor would keep no prints; its fire is cold, so a heat camera would show nothing. Because every test meets a new excuse, no test could ever show the claim to be wrong, and that is why it is not a scientific hypothesis. Sagan asked how such a dragon differs from no dragon at all.

Ideas about the past can be tested too, by the traces the past left behind. Fine-grained rock in China has kept the feathers of small meat-eating dinosaurs as fossils: Sinosauropteryx, described in 1996, was the first, and more than 30 feathered kinds are now known. Asking other scientists would be no test: however many agree, only the evidence can show whether an animal had feathers.

When tests turn out the way a hypothesis predicted, the results support it, even before anyone can explain why it holds. Science never calls an idea proven for good, since a later test under other conditions could still find where it fails.

In everyday talk a theory can be a hunch. To a scientist, a theory is a well-tested explanation of how nature works, backed by evidence from many tests over many years. Germ theory, which explains that tiny living things called germs cause many illnesses, has more than a century of evidence behind it, from Louis Pasteur and Robert Koch onward.

A law sums up a pattern found again and again, often as an equation, and it says what happens without saying why. Hooke's law, stated by Robert Hooke in the 1670s, says that each equal weight hung on a spring adds an equal stretch, until the spring is stretched past its limit.

Isaac Newton's law of gravity, from 1687, tells how hard two masses pull on each other and how the pull fades with distance. Yet Newton later wrote that he had not been able to discover what causes gravity's pull, and he refused to make up a guess. Over two centuries later, Albert Einstein's general relativity, a theory, explained gravity as mass bending space and time.

Boyle's law goes back to Robert Boyle's measurements of 1662: squeezed into less room at the same temperature, a trapped gas presses harder. Boyle himself called the pattern a hypothesis; the name law, for a statement that describes a pattern, came later. The particle theory of gases explains it: a gas's tiny moving particles keep hitting the walls of their container, and crowded closer they hit the walls more often. A law describes a pattern and a theory explains why it happens, so the two do different jobs, and neither one ever grows into the other. The particle theory has equations of its own, yet after more than 150 years of tests it is still a theory.

Many people trust a law more than a theory, as if a law were proven and a theory were not. In fact laws and theories both rest on a great deal of evidence, and both are among the best-tested knowledge in science. Newton's laws of motion describe how forces change motion, and cell theory explains how living things are built. Neither is proven forever: Newton's laws give way to Einstein's relativity for things moving close to the speed of light.
